explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF sends row-count messages to the caller for statements throughout the procedure.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, some run-time errors can leave the transaction around the #DemoCustomers delete open.
@CustomerIdText fixes the customer identifier at N'1' rather than using the supplied @CustomerID.
@OrderID is initialized to business identifier 1, which is then used to filter Sales.Orders.
SELECT * returns every Orders column, including three nvarchar(max) columns, and exposes callers to schema changes.
Nothing determines which ten OrderID values SQL Server returns.
OrderID is the Sales.Orders primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any rows.
NOLOCK can return uncommitted OrderID values or miss or repeat orders during concurrent writes.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) tests a computed value rather than a date range; bounds on OrderDate would allow a range seek if a suitable index exists.
The order filter fixes the reporting year at 2016.
CustomerID is int, so SQL Server implicitly converts the nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText to int for the comparison.
The same predicate must support both all orders and a single CustomerID, which can make one cached plan unsuitable for both cases.
N'%urgent%' requires a substring search through Comments rather than a prefix lookup.
ISNULL wraps the indexed CustomerID in a filter even though the column is NOT NULL and can be compared directly.
The ISNULL expression assigns 0 as an undocumented substitute customer identifier, although the fallback is unreachable in this schema.
The equality test selects customer 1 independently of @CustomerID.
Adding zero to the OrderID primary key introduces an unnecessary expression where a direct key comparison is sufficient.
CustomerID <> 1 can match most orders despite the index on CustomerID.
Customer 1 is permanently excluded by an embedded business identifier.
TOP (1) does not specify which order and customer pair to return.
CROSS JOIN pairs orders with unrelated customers rather than matching each order to its CustomerID.
Any order with a matching order line can supply the single returned OrderID.
Orders and OrderLines are comma-separated, leaving their OrderID relationship in WHERE rather than in a JOIN condition.
The scalar line count depends on each outer OrderID and can require repeated OrderLines lookups.
EXISTS correlates qualifying lines to each outer OrderID. A join to distinct qualifying OrderIDs is equivalent; SQL Server may already use a semi-join.
The qualifying order-line quantity threshold is fixed at 1.
ORDER BY repeats the HasComments CASE expression instead of using its alias, so the two definitions can drift.
ORDER BY 2 refers to OrderDate only while it remains the second select-list item.
Orders sharing an OrderDate have no defined order within the page; OrderID would provide a unique tie-breaker.
The branches select different primary-key values, so UNION's duplicate elimination cannot change the result.
The first branch fixes OrderID at 1.
The second branch fixes OrderID at 2.
The correlated COUNT(*) computes a line count when only the presence of a matching OrderLines row matters.
Multiple orders can assign @OrderID without a defined order, leaving an arbitrary key for later statements; an empty result retains the old value.
The insert can populate @OrderIds with any five orders.
The five orders copied into #ImplicitOrders are not selected in a defined order.
SELECT INTO infers the #ImplicitOrders schema from the query rather than declaring the intended column definition.
The procedure opens a cursor over up to two orders, fetches one arbitrary OrderID, and closes it; no cursor traversal is needed.
The converted @CustomerID is embedded in the SQL text, producing different statement text for different customers.
EXEC runs @Sql without binding CustomerID as a typed parameter.
@OrderID is converted to text and appended to the predicate rather than passed as an int.
sys.sp_executesql receives only the SQL text, with no parameter declaration or bound OrderID.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped, so it remains allocated until procedure scope ends.
The CATCH returns ERROR_MESSAGE() as a result set but does not signal failure to the caller.
The negative OrderID path uses RAISERROR rather than THROW; RAISERROR does not honor XACT_ABORT.
PRINT sends the diagnostic as a potentially buffered client message rather than a structured diagnostic.
The order lookup selects customer 1 rather than using @CustomerID.
The order cutoff is fixed at January 1, 2016, without a parameter or name explaining that boundary.
Without a conversion style, '01/02/2016' can mean January 2 or February 1 depending on DATEFORMAT.
Any order matching an invoice by CustomerID can supply the returned OrderID.
COALESCE wraps o.CustomerID on the Orders side even though this indexed column is NOT NULL.
COALESCE also wraps i.CustomerID on the Invoices side, obscuring the direct comparison on that indexed, NOT NULL column.
The self-join returns one OrderID without defining which order to choose.
Joining Orders to itself on its primary key reproduces the same row and supplies no additional column or filter.
Sorting all orders by the nvarchar(max) Comments column can require substantial memory and spill to tempdb.
SUM(Quantity) must account for every row in Sales.OrderLines because there is no order or date restriction.
OrderID > 0 tests the grouping key, not an aggregate, so it can be expressed as a row filter in WHERE.
The count covers the entire Sales.Orders table on every execution.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns exactly one row, so ordering by OrderCount has no effect.
MERGE adds matching and write complexity even though its only action is a matched update.
The matched action assigns target.Comments to itself, potentially taking write locks and firing update triggers without changing the value.
SET Comments = Comments issues an update on the matching order without changing its data.
Quantity is not a key; the delete removes every matching line across all orders rather than targeting a specific OrderLineID.
The deletion treats quantity -1 as a special value without defining its business meaning.
WAITFOR adds a one-second delay to the write path and keeps the request waiting.
The transaction starts outside a TRY/CATCH boundary, with no error handler to ensure cleanup if control does not reach the rollback.
Sales.Orders has no IDENTITY column in the supplied schema, so enabling IDENTITY_INSERT fails when this branch executes.
sp_who is invoked without its sys schema qualifier.
ROWCOUNT remains 1 for the rest of the procedure, silently limiting later queries and the insert that populates #DemoCustomers.
The category insert relies on the physical order of CategoryID and CategoryName.
The new category is assigned the fixed identifier 99.
The customer insert maps four source expressions to #DemoCustomers by position without naming the target columns.
The pattern always starts with %, preventing a prefix seek on the CustomerName index.
@CustomerName is inserted directly into a quoted SQL literal. A quote in the input can change the executed statement; bind the pattern as a parameter.
sp_executesql is invoked without its sys schema qualifier.
The execution supplies no parameter definition or bound value for the customer-name search.
Every #DemoCustomers row is eligible for the category change. ROWCOUNT 1 caps the update but does not identify an intended customer.
The update assigns the fixed CustomerCategoryID 1 rather than a supplied or looked-up category.
The WHERE test on o.OrderDate rejects NULL-extended rows, so customers without a qualifying order are lost despite the LEFT JOIN.
The order-date filter embeds January 1, 2016 as an unexplained business cutoff.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL does not test for missing values. The column is also NOT NULL, so it cannot contain a missing delivery method.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) can require one scalar function call per returned customer unless SQL Server inlines it.
If the delete or commit fails with a transaction still active, the CATCH does not roll it back and can leave locks held.
The handler selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing or returning failure, so the caller can mistake a failed delete for success.
INDEX = 1 forces the clustered index and prevents the optimizer from choosing the unique CustomerName index for the name filter.
Three nested derived tables pass CustomerID through unchanged; only the innermost query filters rows.
LIKE '%A%' requires a substring search rather than a prefix seek on CustomerName.
SELECT * exposes every column returned by GetCustomerOrdersMulti and makes the result shape depend on the function definition.
GetCustomerOrdersMulti appears to be a multi-statement TVF. If its body is a single relational query, an inline TVF would expose that query to the optimizer.
